claims.text: Git is not GitHub; it is a format of blobs, trees, commits and refs named by their hashes, which GitHub, GitLab, a bare repository and a folder on a laptop all implement.
claims.quote: Git is not GitHub. It is a format: blobs, trees, commits and refs, named by their hashes, laid out in a way any tool can read.

claims.text: sgit is the same kind of thing as git, a standard rather than a server, and the owner thinks that is the most important thing to understand about it.
claims.quote: sgit is the same kind of thing, and I think that is the most important thing to understand about it.

claims.text: People read encrypted git and picture a product with a server in the middle; there is a server, and it is the least interesting part.
claims.quote: There is a server, and it is the least interesting part.

claims.text: A vault is a set of files laid out by a convention: four kinds of object, all ciphertext, blobs, trees, commits and one mutable pointer per branch.
claims.quote: A vault is a set of files laid out by a convention. Four kinds of object, all ciphertext: blobs, the file contents; trees, a folder's encrypted names pointing at blob and tree ids

claims.text: Every object except the ref and the branch index is named by the SHA-256 of its own ciphertext, so a name can never point at different bytes and anyone can keep an object for ever.
claims.quote: Every object except the ref and the branch index is named by the SHA-256 of its own ciphertext, so a name can never point at different bytes

claims.text: The name says which is which: an immutable object's id is obj-cas-imm- and a hash, the mutable pointers are ref-pid-muw- and a hash, so a cache can keep an object without reading it or a header.
claims.quote: An immutable object's id is obj-cas-imm- and a hash; the mutable pointers are ref-pid-muw- and a hash.

claims.text: sgit.ai's documentation pages, a vault read in the browser, fetch 18 objects on a cold load, one 69-byte ref on the next, and nothing inside the two-minute freshness window.
claims.quote: a cold load fetches 18 objects, the next load one 69-byte ref, and a load inside the two-minute freshness window nothing at all.

value.unit: objects fetched on a cold load

claims.text: sgit keeps no deltas between versions of a file; a changed file is a new object, a trade made so anyone can cache without asking.
claims.quote: sgit keeps no deltas between versions of a file; a changed file is a new object.

claims.text: The vault key gives the vault id and, one way, the read key; the read key cannot be turned back into the write key, so it can be published.
claims.quote: The read key cannot be turned back into the write key, so it can be published.

claims.text: The read key gives the ref's name: the first twelve hex characters of an HMAC of the read key over sg-vault-v1:file-id:ref: and the vault id, so the server never told you where the head is.
claims.quote: In the CLI's code it is the first twelve hex characters of an HMAC of the read key over sg-vault-v1:file-id:ref: and the vault id.

claims.text: A file is four kinds of request from its read key, ref, commit, the trees on the path and the blob, and every one is a plain GET of a fixed path.
claims.quote: a file is four kinds of request from its read key, and every one is a plain GET of a fixed path.

value.unit: GETs from read key to file

claims.text: Writing is the same objects PUT in batches, plus one compare-and-swap on the ref and the branch index.
claims.quote: Writing is the same objects, PUT in batches, and one compare-and-swap on the ref and the branch index.

claims.text: Two independent implementations speak the format, the CLI and the browser vault app, and each verifies the other's changes.
claims.quote: Two independent implementations speak this format: the CLI, and the browser vault app

claims.text: A standard is a format with more than one implementation that agree.
claims.quote: That is what a standard is: a format with more than one implementation that agree.

claims.text: Any storage that answers a GET implements the read half of the convention: an S3 bucket, a CDN, GitHub Pages, a folder, Python's one-line file server.
claims.quote: any storage that answers a GET implements the read half of the convention: an S3 bucket, a CDN, GitHub Pages, a folder, Python's one-line file server.

claims.text: This site measured 317 milliseconds a request through the vault API against 44 for a small file from GitHub Pages.
claims.quote: 317 milliseconds a request through the vault API, against 44 for a small file from GitHub Pages.

value.unit: milliseconds a request through the vault API, against 44 from GitHub Pages

claims.text: Stripped down, the API has two jobs: protect writes with an access token and the compare-and-swap, and shorten reads a little with batches of fifty objects and a listing.
claims.quote: the API has two jobs: protect writes, with an access token and the compare-and-swap, and shorten reads a little, with batches of fifty objects

claims.text: Every deployment option is shipped: a folder, a laptop running the hosted image with sgit serve in Docker, Podman or Python, your own server, a static host, or the hosted service, a Lambda in front of S3 behind CloudFront.
claims.quote: a laptop, with sgit serve running the hosted service's own image in Docker, Podman or a plain Python process

claims.text: How fast sgit is depends on how close the storage is: on the vault behind this newsroom a one-folder clone is 13 seconds hosted and 0.8 seconds from a local server.
claims.quote: a one-folder clone is 13 seconds hosted and 0.8 seconds from a local server

value.unit: seconds for a one-folder clone hosted, against 0.8 locally

claims.text: On ruv.sgit.ai's hive runs, on a local server, every operation takes between 0.4 and 1.5 seconds, most of it starting Python and deriving the key.
claims.quote: every operation takes between 0.4 and 1.5 seconds, most of it starting Python and deriving the key.

value.unit: seconds, upper bound per operation on ruv.sgit.ai's local server

claims.text: The cache layer is shipped: sgit cache add declares a path, and every push keeps an encrypted cache object for it at a location derived from the read key and the path, so a reader needs no walk.
claims.quote: every push keeps an encrypted cache object for it at a location derived from the read key and the path.

claims.text: A miss or a stale cache entry falls back to the ordinary walk, so correctness never depends on the cache; losing one is a performance problem, never a correctness one.
claims.quote: A miss or a stale entry falls back to the ordinary walk, so correctness never depends on the cache

claims.text: The cache layer is Scion's derived data, built by the writer instead of a server and named by the key instead of indexed by it.
claims.quote: This is Scion's "derived data", built by the writer instead of a server, and named by the key instead of indexed by it.

claims.text: sgit keeps history, blame and merges on the client, and would even if the server could read, because a merge is a workflow step that needs the context, the history and the policy on who may merge.
claims.quote: a merge is a workflow step that needs the context of the change, the history and the policy that says who may merge what.

claims.text: Scion's post concedes the point from the other side: it could not keep a merge queue at its rate, so concurrent changes can conflict and Claude typically fixes them.
claims.quote: concurrent changes can conflict, but Claude can typically fix these conflicts

claims.text: sgit keeps the property that made git git, a full clone as a complete verifiable copy, but the full clone became optional through folder scope, history depth, sparse clones and the cache layer.
claims.quote: What changed is that the full clone became optional.

claims.text: None of this was a plan to be minimal: because the server cannot read a byte, every feature had to be expressible as objects a writer produces and a reader derives, which is why the designs are small enough to be a standard.
claims.quote: None of this was a plan to be minimal. The server cannot read a byte, so "just do it on the server" was never available

claims.text: sgit is not a formal standard: no standards body, a documented format with two implementations.
claims.quote: Not a formal standard. No standards body; a documented format with two implementations.

claims.text: It is not proven at Scion's scale; the largest vault in daily use is about 35,000 objects and ten agents.
claims.quote: Not proven at Scion's scale. The largest vault in daily use is about 35,000 objects and ten agents.

claims.text: There is no blame or bisect yet, and a partial clone of a long history walks the commits one at a time until a commit-chain object ships; a depth avoids it today.
claims.quote: No blame or bisect yet. And a partial clone of a long history walks the commits one at a time until a commit-chain object ships

claims.text: The CDN in front of the hosted API does not cache object reads yet; browsers, clients and static hosts do.
claims.quote: The CDN in front of the hosted API does not cache object reads yet. Browsers, clients and static hosts do.
